content: The Intrauterine System (IUS) is a hormonal contraceptive device that is inserted into the uterus. It contains a hormone-releasing cylinder that emits levonorgestrel, a type of progestin. Currently, the only available brand is the T-frame LNG-20 IUS, marketed as the Mirena Coil by Schering Health and Berlex Laboratories. In the UK, the term IUS is used to differentiate hormonal intrauterine contraceptives from copper or silver-based intrauterine devices (IUDs). In the US, no such distinction is made, and all intrauterine contraceptives are referred to as IUDs. Clinical Uses The IUS is used for contraception and to manage conditions such as menorrhagia (heavy periods), endometriosis, chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, and anemia. In some cases, its use may prevent the need for a hysterectomy. Fitting The IUS must be inserted by a qualified medical professional following the manufacturer’s instructions and using aseptic techniques to prevent bacterial contamination of the uterus. Antibiotics are recommended before insertion for women at high risk of endocarditis but are not routinely used. During the procedure, the cervix is dilated to measure the uterus and insert the device. Cervical dilation can be uncomfortable or painful, and painkillers are often advised beforehand. Insertion is generally more comfortable mid-cycle when the cervix is naturally dilated. Once in place, the IUS is approved for up to five years of contraceptive use. Mechanisms of Contraception The Mirena IUS releases 20 micrograms of levonorgestrel daily. Its exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, but it is believed to work through several effects: It reduces the frequency of ovulation. It alters cervical mucus, making it difficult for sperm to pass through the cervix. The presence of the device in the uterus triggers the release of leukocytes and prostaglandins by the endometrium, which are hostile to sperm and eggs. It thins the endometrium, potentially inhibiting embryo implantation, though this theory has not been definitively proven. Removal IUS removal is typically easiest at the end of a woman’s menstrual period. A doctor or trained nurse uses forceps to grasp the IUS threads and gently retract the device. If the threads are not visible or cannot be felt during routine checks, an ultrasound may be required to locate the device and rule out uterine perforation or expulsion. Rarely, hysteroscopy may be needed. Fertility generally returns to normal within a few months after removal, with approximately 80% of women able to conceive within 12 months. Contraindications The insertion of a levonorgestrel IUS is not recommended in certain conditions due to unacceptable health risks. These include: Pregnancy Postpartum puerperal sepsis Immediately post-septic abortion Unexplained vaginal bleeding suspected to be a serious condition Malignant gestational trophoblastic disease Cervical cancer awaiting treatment Active liver disease (e.g., acute viral hepatitis, severe cirrhosis, liver tumors) Current or recent breast cancer (hormonally sensitive tumors) Endometrial cancer Uterine cavity distortions caused by fibroids or anatomical abnormalities Current pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) Current purulent cervicitis, chlamydial infection, or gonorrheal STIs Known pelvic tuberculosis Side Effects and Complications Location of Device The IUS may be expelled through the cervix after insertion, with an expulsion rate of 4% observed in clinical trials, most occurring within the first year. Expulsion is more common in younger women, nulliparous women, and those who have had the device inserted immediately after childbirth or abortion. Uterine perforation is a rare but serious complication that can occur during insertion or later due to device migration. Perforation may cause internal scarring, infection, or damage to other organs and may require surgery. Both expulsion and perforation result in loss of contraceptive efficacy. Women are advised to check the position of the IUS threads at least once per menstrual cycle or monthly if they do not menstruate. If the threads are problematic during intercourse, they can be adjusted or shortened by a healthcare provider. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease and STIs PID, often caused by sexually transmitted infections (STIs), is a serious condition that can lead to infertility. Women with STIs are at increased risk of PID if they use an IUD. Therefore, IUDs are not recommended for women at high risk of STIs, such as those with multiple sexual partners or partners with multiple partners. While animal studies suggested that progestin-only contraceptives like Mirena might increase the risk of HIV transmission due to vaginal wall thinning, human studies have not confirmed this. However, the IUS does not protect against STIs. Postpartum and Post-Abortion Insertion The IUS can be inserted immediately postpartum (within 48 hours). However, delayed insertion (after 48 hours) increases the risk of uterine perforation if uterine involution is incomplete. Involution typically completes by 4-6 weeks postpartum. Special considerations apply to breastfeeding women. Insertion is not recommended for women who have had a second-trimester abortion within the past four weeks or a medical abortion without confirmation of completion or first menstruation. Expulsion is more common when the IUS is inserted immediately after childbirth or abortion. Hormonal Side Effects Localized Menstrual periods often become lighter or stop completely within one year of IUS use in about 20% of women. Irregular bleeding is common in the first few months, with an average of 16 days of bleeding or spotting in the first month, decreasing to about four days by 12 months. Systemic The progestin in the IUS is released at a lower dose than other progestin-only contraceptives. Enlarged ovarian follicles (ovarian cysts) have been diagnosed in about 12% of IUS users. Most are asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously within 2-3 months without requiring surgical intervention. Nursing Mothers There is an increased risk of uterine perforation in lactating women. Progestin-only contraceptives like the IUS are not believed to affect milk supply or infant growth. However, some studies have shown lower breastfeeding continuation rates among IUS users compared to copper IUD users. Levonorgestrel is found in nursing infants at 7% of the maternal concentration. Long-term effects on infants exposed to levonorgestrel through breast milk have not been studied extensively. Recommendations for IUS use during breastfeeding vary, with some organizations advising against immediate postpartum insertion due to increased expulsion rates and potential effects on infant development. Pregnancy Although the IUS is highly effective, it is not 100% reliable. If pregnancy occurs, the presence of the IUD increases the risk of miscarriage and preterm delivery, particularly in the second trimester. These risks are mitigated if the IUD is removed after pregnancy is detected. Ectopic pregnancies occur in approximately 1 per 1000 users per year. Bone Density No evidence suggests that the IUS affects bone mineral density (BMD). A study of long-term users found no significant differences in BMD compared to non-users of similar age and BMI. Types of Intrauterine Systems The first hormonal uterine device, Progestasert, was developed in 1976 and contained progesterone released at 65 micrograms per day. It was replaced annually in most countries and had a failure rate of 2% per year. The Mirena Coil was developed in the 1970s and is distributed by Schering Health and Berlex Laboratories. It releases 20 micrograms of levonorgestrel daily and is approved for five years of use. Other devices, such as Femilis and FibroPlant-LNG, are under development, offering lower doses and frameless designs.
